issue_context.title: Wrong assertion on tests
issue_context.body:
Golang does not allow to call certain testing methods in goroutines

> New warning for invalid testing.T use in goroutines[¶](https://go.dev/doc/go1.16#vet-testing-T)
The vet tool now warns about invalid calls to the testing.T method Fatal from within a goroutine created during the test. This also warns on calls to Fatalf, FailNow, and Skip{,f,Now} methods on testing.T tests or testing.B benchmarks.

As consequence, framework that calls this methods internally can not be used in goroutines, this is the case. with testify https://github.com/stretchr/testify/issues/772#issuecomment-945166599

> Document in the assert package that failing assertions will call t.Errorf().
> Document in the testify (module root) package that require is not appropriate in a goroutine but assert is.


It seems there is a linter that helps to identify this incorrect usage https://github.com/Antonboom/testifylint#go-require

If this occurs, mutator is going to be nil, leading to panic below in the `mutator.Admit`.

This PR satisfies the linter, but it doesn't really fix these tests. The test binary still crashes if something goes wrong instead of just failing the test.

The same problem occurs pretty much everywhere where `require` was replaced with a merely logging a failure and then continuing as if the failure hadn't happened.
This is part of why I like the standard Go testing - Error and Fatalf are far more obvious than assert and require, to my eyes
But this is now using `t.Error`, and it's wrong here!?
```Go
mutator, ok := handler.(MutationInterface)
if !ok {
	t.Error("handler is not an interface of type MutationInterface")
}
...
  ... mutator.Admit(ctx, a, nil) ... // <- this panics after an error.
```
And just to be clear, the panic then aborts the entire process, not just the test in which it occurs.
Yeah, people still get this wrong, but at least I don't have to look up which of assert or require means fatal.
To me, "require" was always the obviously stronger variant, but I get your point. Perhaps we should use testify more often so that everyone remains familiar with it? :stuck_out_tongue_closed_eyes: 

> It looks like a number of Errorf should perhaps be Fatalf

Except that this would be wrong in a goroutine.

Perhaps `t.Error + return` works, as long as this then doesn't cause a timeout in the main test goroutine. If the main goroutine is waiting for work done in the helper goroutine, then the abnormal condition should be communicated back to the main goroutine to ensure swift execution of the tests.

The point is, `require` cannot be mechanically replaced. Removing it does not automatically "fix" the test. One has to look at each individual usage and think about how the test should fail when an assertion is not satisfied.
@my-git9: will you follow up on this? Do we need an issue to avoid forgetting about it?

The alternative is to revert the PR. Then we can find potentially problematic calls through the linter and fix them differently. As it stands now, the linter is not complaining but the tests still misbehave in case of an errors.

I don't like that because it is good to have this check enabled for new tests.

I will open an issue and get this fixed, independently of the discussion, we need to fix it
but is better to fail the entire suite if a test fails, than to pass ... the later will go unnoticed forever, the former will be detected immediately
